title: Johns Hopkins Hospital Study Abroad Report
paragraphs: [Introduction] What made me want to go on this exchange program was that it was introduced on the evening news when I was either a junior high school or high school student. I am very happy that my long-held wish has come true, and now that I am back, I feel I want to move on to the next step building on this study abroad. I studied abroad at Johns Hopkins Hospital from April 20 to June 17. From April 20 to May 20 I rotated through pediatric oncology, and from May 23 to June 17 through oncology (adult). It is an oncology-heavy combination, but this was not my own request; it came about this way because of Hopkins' circumstances. However, when I actually rotated, both departments were very interesting, and thinking about it now, it was very good.

[Pediatric Oncology] The schedule through the day began with handover from the night shift, followed by sit down rounds (morning conference), walk rounds, a lunchtime lecture, and an afternoon lecture for residents. In my free time I looked at charts in the residents' room and asked the residents questions. The diseases handled in pediatric oncology are varied, and there are many patients with leukemia, brain tumors, osteosarcoma and so on. What impressed me especially were the rounds, where doctors, nurses, pharmacists and dietitians discussed actively together and thought about treatment plans. However, pediatric oncology was apparently a department that had hardly ever accepted students before, so I was given no assignments and was rarely asked questions, and I was often at a loss about what to do. Before the rotation I had imagined that clerkships at Hopkins would mean being given various assignments every day and moving around without a moment to breathe. A feeling of impatience arose, that "I have to do something on my own," and after that I asked to be assigned patients and gradually began to ask questions on my own. What especially troubled me during the clerkship was the number of abbreviations. Because very many drugs are used in chemotherapy, reading the charts was a struggle. Using that information to give a patient presentation at the morning conference without disrupting its flow was a continuous source of tension. After the conference, being told "Your presentation was very good" made me truly happy. When I observed the outpatient clinic, they were celebrating a boy completing the course of chemotherapy for osteosarcoma that he had been receiving for about three years (a "chemo party"). There was singing and an enormous cake, very American, was presented, and watching the happy faces of the boy and his family, tears came naturally. On the other hand, a girl with a local recurrence of osteosarcoma arising in the pelvis was admitted to the ward. In this case the prognosis is very poor, and the girl herself knew it and cried every day. She and her family were very downcast, and it became an event in which I witnessed the hardship of pediatric oncology.

[Oncology] The team I was on mainly handled solid tumors. Almost all patients had metastatic tumors. On rounds I saw many times patients being told by the attending that there was no prospect of cure whatever treatment was given, and while I was reminded of how frightening cancer is, I was also spurred with the desire to develop new treatments. Because every patient had serious problems of their own in this way, rounds sometimes lasted four hours. Many patients who come to Hopkins have very high expectations that "since I have come to the best medical facility, I should be cured," and so the responsibility on the doctors' side seemed heavy and hard. Indeed, the Hopkins residents are of a very high level, and I hear that matching there is very difficult. I was always assigned one patient, and did the pre-rounds in the morning and presented. By the second month I had gotten used to the Hopkins system and gradually became able to catch the fast conversations between doctors. However, there were several times when a nurse asked me a question about a drug order and I could not answer, and each time I felt frustrated. There was also a student from the Dominican Republic who was visiting oncology for a month, who was a great stimulus. She was going to graduate from medical school this summer, and planned to spend a year studying for the USMLE and aim to match into a US residency. Her English ability and motivation were high, and I found myself wondering, if I were to work in the United States, whether I could work in such a competitive environment. Compared with pediatric oncology, oncology was more used to students, so to speak, and more educational, and the teaching, on palliative treatment of terminal cancer, immunotherapy, tumor lysis syndrome and so on, was full of interesting topics and was a lot of fun.

[Summary of the Study Abroad] From Hopkins' reputation, I had thought I would hardly be able to interact with local students. However, by mustering just a little more courage than usual, I was able to create such opportunities as often as I liked. I asked to take part in an emergency simulation class, I sneaked into a social gathering for undergraduates, and I am glad I could take on various challenges that I would have hesitated over and given up on in Japan. The students I became friends with through this were very kind to me, and it is a very good memory that they showed me around cities near Baltimore by car. Setting aside Baltimore's public safety (laughs), I am truly glad I was able to come to Hopkins. Through this study abroad I was able to meet various people and have wonderful experiences. I am very grateful to everyone who supported me in studying abroad. From now on I would like to make use of this experience so that I can repay those who supported me.
